explanations.explanation: Paul says it plainly: “…death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.” (Romans 5:12) Adam, the first man, is where it started, but he isn't the only name on the list. I think that's why Paul goes so far back, so nobody in the room feels singled out. Hold onto your hat, friend, because the good news is coming.

explanations.answer: Adam alone because he sinned first
explanations.explanation: Adam did go first, and sin entered the world through him. But Paul doesn't stop there. He says death was passed on to all men, because all sinned. Adam's the first cookie out of the oven, friend, not the whole batch.

explanations.answer: Israel alone because it had the law
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't tie death to Israel or to the law. He says death was passed on to all men. He even says death reigned from Adam until Moses, and Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one the law came through (John 1:17). Death never waited around for the law to show up.

Paul says death reigned from Adam until Moses. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one the law came through: “For the law was given through Moses…” (John 1:17). So Paul's point is that death was already running things before any law was handed down. Nobody had to write it up for death to show up.

Noah, who built the ark as God commanded him (Genesis 6:22), is a great name, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says death reigned from Adam until Moses. Moses is the marker because that's where the law comes into the picture. Good guess, friend, just the wrong stop on the timeline.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), comes along way after the spot Paul has in mind. Paul says death reigned from Adam until Moses. He's talking about the stretch before the law was given. David's a fine name, but he's too late for this one.

Paul says the opposite. Death reigned “…even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed.” (Romans 5:14) So death's reach went past the people who copied Adam's exact move. It's a bigger reign than that.

That's right, and here's what Paul says: death reigned “…even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed.” (Romans 5:14) Death didn't keep a guest list. It reigned from Adam until Moses, and that included people who never did what Adam did.

Paul names Him right in the next verse: “…the one man, Jesus Christ.” (Romans 5:15) Adam is a pattern, and Jesus is who the pattern points to. One man's act reached the many, and so does the other's. I stamp patterns for a living, and even I didn't see that one coming.

Abraham, who God called to leave his home (Genesis 12:1), is a huge name in the Bible, but Paul isn't pointing to him here. In the very next verse Paul names the One: “…the one man, Jesus Christ.” (Romans 5:15) Adam is the pattern, and Jesus is the One to come.

Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12), isn't who Paul has in mind. Paul spells out the answer in the next verse: “…the one man, Jesus Christ.” (Romans 5:15) Adam is the pattern, and Jesus is the One it points to. Nice try, friend, but this crown goes to somebody else.

Paul says the opposite: “But the gift is not like the trespass.” (Romans 5:15) The two sit side by side, but they don't match. The gift through Jesus Christ goes far past the trespass. That's the whole twist, friend.

That's right. Paul says it flat out: “But the gift is not like the trespass.” (Romans 5:15) They sit side by side, but they aren't equals. Then he says how much more God's grace and the gift abound to the many.

Paul's words are “…how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many!” (Romans 5:15) He's got his hands in the air on that one. The trespass was real, but grace goes further. I'd be waving my mustache too.

Paul does say the many died by the trespass of the one man. But he sets that down so he can say how much more grace and the gift abound to the many. The trespass is the starting line in this comparison, not the finish.

Death did reign, and Paul doesn't downplay that. But he sets it up as the thing grace goes beyond. His words are “…how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many!” (Romans 5:15) Death has a long reign, but grace outruns it.

Paul's word is justification: “…the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification.” (Romans 5:16) It's the opposite of condemnation. Think about that: it followed many trespasses, not just one. A gift that gets bigger when the pile gets bigger is the best kind of math, friend.

The list got longer, but that's not where Paul lands. He says the judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification. The gift doesn't add charges, it answers them. Nobody's pulling out a bigger clipboard.

Paul doesn't talk about a warning here. He says “…the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification.” (Romans 5:16) A gift and a warning are two very different things to find in a box. This one is a gift.

Paul says it just that way: “…those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!” (Romans 5:17) Death reigned through one man, and now life reigns through another. Notice the word receive, friend. It's a gift, so the job is to take it.

Paul really does say it: “…those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!” (Romans 5:17) Death reigned through one man, and life reigns through the other. It's a gift, so the job is to receive it.

Paul says “…so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.” (Romans 5:18) One trespass on one side, one act of righteousness on the other. It's a clean match, and it ends with life.

Worship is a good word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says “…so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.” (Romans 5:18) The matching pair is trespass and righteousness. Worship never makes it into this verse.

Judgment does show up in this passage, but on the other side of the scale. Paul says the judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation (Romans 5:16). Here the match for the trespass is “…one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.” (Romans 5:18)

Paul says the many were made sinners “…through the disobedience of the one man…” (Romans 5:19). One man's disobedience, and it reached the many. It's a heavy word, but it sets up the turn that's coming.

Paul says the many will be made righteous “…through the obedience of the one man…” (Romans 5:19). Disobedience on one side, obedience on the other. That's the swap, and it's the best one in the whole passage.

Pride is a real thing, but Paul doesn't name it here. He says it was Adam's disobedience that made the many sinners (Romans 5:19). I won't guess at what was going on inside Adam. I'll stick with the word Paul gives.

Paul doesn't mention anger in this verse. He says the many were made sinners through the disobedience of the one man, and the many will be made righteous through the obedience of the one man (Romans 5:19). Those are the two words that go in the blanks.
Weakness isn't the word Paul uses. In this verse, it's disobedience on one side and obedience on the other (Romans 5:19). That's the pair, and it fits the pattern from top to bottom.

Paul says the opposite: “The law came in so that the trespass would increase…” (Romans 5:20) Increase, not shrink. That sounds backwards at first, and it made me lean over my counter too. Keep reading, because the next part is the good part.
That's right. Paul says “The law came in so that the trespass would increase…” (Romans 5:20) Increase, not shrink. It sounds backwards at first, but he's not done with the sentence yet.

Paul says “…where sin increased, grace increased all the more…” (Romans 5:20) However high sin got, grace went higher. If I could stamp that on a cookie, I'd need a stamper the size of the Dorinverse.
Paul says the opposite. “…where sin increased, grace increased all the more…” (Romans 5:20) Grace doesn't back away from sin. It goes right to the spot where sin piled up and gives more.
Staying even sounds fair, but that's not what Paul says. He says “…where sin increased, grace increased all the more…” (Romans 5:20) All the more is beyond even. Grace doesn't tie, friend.

Paul says “…just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” (Romans 5:21) Sin reigned in death, and that's the first blank. It's the low note he sets up so the next one can ring out.

Paul says “…so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” (Romans 5:21) Sin had its reign, and now grace gets one. This one ends in eternal life, friend. I'm doing a little hop on my gold base.
Fear doesn't show up in this verse. Paul says sin reigned in death, and grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life (Romans 5:21). Fear isn't reigning anywhere in that sentence.

Wrath isn't the word Paul uses here. He says sin reigned in death, and grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 5:21). The pair he lines up is sin and grace.
Paul doesn't use shame in this verse. He says sin reigned in death, and grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life (Romans 5:21). Those are the two that go in the blanks.
